chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Yunus ibn Yaqoub, from Suleyman ibn Khalid, who said:

I attended the evening meal of Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) in the summer, and a platter was brought with bread, and a bowl of tharid (bread soaked in broth) and meat was brought. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Come to me with this food.' So I approached, and he placed his hand in it and raised it while saying: 'I seek refuge with Allah from the Fire, I seek refuge with Allah from the Fire, I seek refuge with Allah from the Fire. This is what we cannot be patient with, so how (will we be patient with) the Fire? This is what we do not have the strength to bear, so how (will we bear) the Fire? This is what we cannot endure, so how (will we endure) the Fire?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And he (peace be upon him) repeated that until the food was manageable, so he ate and we ate with him.'

key_terms.أَسْتَجِيرُ: I seek refuge/protection: A form of du'a asking for safety from a specific danger.
key_terms.النَّار: The Fire: Referring to Jahannam (Hellfire), a central concept in Islamic eschatology.
key_terms.ثَرِيد: Tharid: A dish of bread soaked in meat broth, a common staple in early Islamic times.
key_terms.نَصْبِرُ: We are patient: Referring to the endurance required for trials or sensations.
key_terms.نَقْوَى: We have strength: Referring to physical or spiritual capacity to bear a burden.

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) say while touching hot food to illustrate patience in the afterlife?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) utilizes the immediate physical sensation of heat from fresh food as a tangible metaphor (*tamthil*) for the intensity of Hellfire, illustrating the principle of *al-adghal min al-akbar* (the lesser from the greater). By repeatedly seeking refuge in Allah while touching the hot dish, he emphasizes that if humans struggle to endure minor worldly discomforts, they will certainly require divine protection against the severe trials of the Hereafter. This narrative underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on deriving theological insights from mundane daily activities, linking physical endurance to spiritual resilience.
